---
title: "Follow-up windows and death"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  eval = FALSE
)
```

A time-to-event outcome needs three things: a start, an event date, and a
date until which the person was watched. SRTR files supply all three, but
from different sources that do not always agree. This article shows where
they disagree and what that does to an analysis. The companion article,
[Follow-up forms are reports, not events](follow-up-forms.html), covers what
the forms themselves record.

As there, the code is not run on this website because it needs real SAFs.
Run it on your own files, compare the naive version with the sRtr one, and
share counts only, masking any count under 11 with the `mask()` and
`mask_n()` helpers below. As explained in the companion article, also avoid
sharing counts whose difference is small: subtraction undoes the masking.

```{r setup}
library(sRtr)
library(dplyr)

set_srtr_wd("path/to/your/SAFs")
tx <- load_srtr_file("TX_LI")

# Counts safe to share: any count from 1 to 10 shows as "<11".
mask_n <- function(n) {
  noquote(ifelse(n > 0 & n < 11, "<11", format(n, big.mark = ",")))
}
# The same for a frequency table of a column.
mask <- function(x) mask_n(table(x, useNA = "ifany"))
```

**A note on `add_time_to_event_outcomes()`.** It builds the death, graft
failure, malignancy and rejection outcomes described here. It is not yet
exported, so this article calls it as `sRtr:::add_time_to_event_outcomes()`;
its name and columns may change before it is. The other functions used here
are exported.

# Events count only while someone is watching

Follow-up forms keep arriving after a recipient's last follow-up date
(`TFL_LAFUDATE`), and some are dated after death. A report outside the
period the recipient was followed for cannot be paired with the right
censoring: everyone else's follow-up ends at their last follow-up date.
SRTR's own graft survival estimates follow this rule for most organs. Their
follow-up is censored at the last OPTN follow-up date, and for lung and
heart-lung they "do not include deaths that occur after loss to follow-up
in the OPTN database" ([SRTR Technical Methods](#ref-psr)).

SAFs also hold `TFL_ENDTXFU` (labeled "Cohort date" in the data
dictionary), which SRTR staff describe as "the variable to
use to identify the last possible follow-up date" for each recipient, with a
three-month lag to allow forms to be completed
([Kim and Snyder 2012](#ref-kim2012), slide 25). sRtr does not use it yet.
Compare it with `TFL_LAFUDATE` in your files.

```{r window, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 2.6, fig.alt = "Timeline for three made-up recipients, in years since transplant, each with a shaded window from transplant to the earlier of last follow-up and death. Recipient A has a malignancy report at year 2, inside the window, which counts. Recipient B's window ends at last follow-up at year 3, and a report at year 3.5 falls outside it and does not count. Recipient C died at year 2.5; a report dated on the day of death is flagged, and one dated after death does not count."}
windows <- data.frame(who = c("A", "B", "C"), end = c(4, 3, 2.5))
reports <- data.frame(
  who = c("A", "B", "C", "C"),
  year = c(2, 3.5, 2.5, 3.2),
  kind = c("Counts", "Outside the window", "Day of death (flagged)",
           "Outside the window")
)
reports$kind <- factor(
  reports$kind,
  c("Counts", "Day of death (flagged)", "Outside the window")
)
ends <- data.frame(
  who = c("A", "B", "C"), year = c(4, 3, 2.5),
  label = c("Last follow-up", "Last follow-up", "Death")
)
ink <- "#52514e"

ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = windows,
    ggplot2::aes(x = 0, xend = end, y = who, yend = who),
    linewidth = 6, colour = "#cde2fb", lineend = "butt"
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = ends,
    ggplot2::aes(x = year - 0.05, y = who, label = label),
    nudge_y = 0.3, hjust = 1, size = 3.1, colour = ink
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(
    data = ends,
    ggplot2::aes(x = year, xend = year, y = as.numeric(factor(who, c("C", "B", "A"))) - 0.18,
                 yend = as.numeric(factor(who, c("C", "B", "A"))) + 0.18),
    colour = ink, linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = reports,
    ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = who, colour = kind, shape = kind),
    size = 3.5, stroke = 1.2
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Counts" = "#eb6834",
      "Day of death (flagged)" = "#2a78d6",
      "Outside the window" = "#8a8984"
    ),
    name = "Malignancy report"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "Counts" = 17,
      "Day of death (flagged)" = 15,
      "Outside the window" = 4
    ),
    name = "Malignancy report"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_discrete(limits = c("C", "B", "A")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    "Years since transplant", breaks = 0:4, limits = c(0, 4.3)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(y = "Recipient") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.justification = "left"
  )
```

**The naive approach** feeds the first report and the last follow-up date
straight into `srtr_time_to_event()`:

```{r}
naive <- tx |>
  add_txf_outcomes() |>
  srtr_time_to_event(
    event_date = FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE,
    start_date = REC_TX_DT,
    censor_date = TFL_LAFUDATE,
    prefix = "MALIG",
    units = "days"
  )
```

`srtr_time_to_event()` is a low-level tool: it trusts the dates it is given.
Any non-missing event date counts, even one after the censoring date. So
this counts reports dated after last follow-up and after death, and it
censors recipients who died without a report at their last follow-up date,
which may be after their death. Look at how often that happens in your
files:

```{r}
naive <- srtr_composite_death(naive)
naive |>
  summarise(
    report_after_last_follow_up = sum(FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE > TFL_LAFUDATE, na.rm = TRUE),
    report_after_death = sum(FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE > REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE, na.rm = TRUE),
    report_on_day_of_death = sum(FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE == REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), mask_n))
```

**With sRtr**, malignancy and rejection count only from the transplant date
to the earlier of the last follow-up date and death from any source, both
inclusive. A recipient without a counted event is censored at the end of
that window. A report outside it stays in its date column, so you can see
what was left out:

```{r}
out <- sRtr:::add_time_to_event_outcomes(tx)

left_out <- !is.na(out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE) & out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_BINARY == 0
mask_n(sum(left_out))
```

With no last follow-up date, the end of the window is unknown. sRtr does
not use the death date in its place, because the forms do not show that
the recipient was followed up to death; the time is missing instead.

# Reports dated on the day of death

On real files, a large number of first malignancy and rejection reports
carry the same date as the recipient's death. Such a report may come from
the form filed at death: the malignancy may then have been present well
before that date, or the report may describe what was found at death. The
flag only compares two dates; it says nothing about whether the malignancy
caused the death, which needs cause-of-death data.

sRtr counts these reports by default, since they fall inside the window,
and flags them so you can test how much they matter:

```{r}
mask(out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_DEATH_DAY)
```

A sensitivity analysis should keep the cohort and everyone's follow-up time
the same, and change only the counted events dated on the day of death.
Dropping those recipients instead would also throw away all their earlier
time at risk. Because their window already ends at death, their time is
the same either way; only the event indicator changes:

```{r}
reclassified <- out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_DEATH_DAY %in% TRUE &
  out$FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_BINARY %in% 1L
sensitivity <- out |>
  mutate(
    MALIG_SENS_BINARY = if_else(reclassified, 0L, FIRST_FU_MALIG_DATE_BINARY)
  )
mask_n(sum(reclassified))
```

These recipients are then censored at death. Death is a competing event
for malignancy: say which estimand you want. A cause-specific hazard
treats death as censoring, as here; a cumulative incidence needs death
coded as a competing event, for example with an Aalen-Johansen
estimator. The complement of a Kaplan-Meier curve overstates the
cumulative incidence when there are competing events
([Austin et al. 2016](#ref-austin); [Noordzij et al. 2013](#ref-noordzij)).
[Sapir-Pichhadze et al. 2016](#ref-sapir) work through both approaches,
cause-specific and subdistribution hazards, with SRTR data.

# Which death date?

Death is recorded in three places: the OPTN record
(`PERS_OPTN_DEATH_DT`), the Social Security death data
(`PERS_SSA_DEATH_DT`) and the follow-up forms (`TFL_DEATH_DT`). They do not
always agree.

The Social Security date is "determined from SSA database" (data
dictionary). SRTR and OPTN "receive monthly updates from the NTIS Death
Master File" ([The SRTR Database](#ref-srtrdb)). Since 2011 the
Death Master File has excluded many state-reported deaths. It misses a
varying share of deaths across states and over time, so it should not be
used on its own ([da Graca et al. 2013](#ref-dagraca);
[Navar et al. 2019](#ref-navar)).

**The naive approach** picks one source, often the OPTN date, and misses
deaths recorded only elsewhere. Picking the earliest of the three is not
safe either: one wrong early date then moves that death.

**With sRtr**, `srtr_composite_death()` takes the first available date in a
fixed order (OPTN, then SSA, then the forms), records the source, and flags
recipients whose sources disagree. `add_spread_days = TRUE` adds how far
apart they are:

```{r}
d <- srtr_composite_death(tx, add_spread_days = TRUE)
mask(d$REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE_source)
mask(cut(
  d$REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE_spread_days,
  c(-1, 0, 1, 7, 30, Inf),
  labels = c("agree", "1 day", "2-7 days", "8-30 days", "more")
))
```

On real files, most disagreements are a few days, but some are months or
years. `conflict_days` sets how far apart the sources may be before the
flag is raised; the default, 0, flags any difference. A larger tolerance is
your choice of what counts as recording noise. Even a one-day difference
can matter when the question is about order: whether a graft failed before
the recipient died, or a report fell before death.

The order of sources is itself a choice. sRtr and the current SRTR
program-specific reports both put OPTN first: "the OPTN death date takes
precedence" ([SRTR Technical Methods](#ref-psr)). After that they differ.
The reports choose between the Social Security Death Master File and CMS
("the SSDMF date takes precedence"); sRtr uses Social Security and then the
follow-up form, and has no CMS date. Older SRTR guidance started from the
form date for the transplant (`TFL_DEATH_DT`), then OPTN, Social Security
and CMS ([Kim and Snyder 2012](#ref-kim2012), slide 26). In the liver
release documented in `?srtr_composite_death`, the form and OPTN dates
agreed on the same day for over 99% of recipients who had both, so the two
orders rarely give different dates.

# Deaths found after follow-up ends

Transplant programs need not report deaths after the required follow-up
intervals: they "may voluntarily submit death dates after these defined
follow-up intervals, but they are not required to do so"
([The SRTR Database](#ref-srtrdb)). The Social Security data, by contrast,
find deaths long after a recipient stops being followed. If those deaths
count as events but survivors are censored at
their last follow-up date, the dead are followed for longer than the
living, and mortality is overstated.

```{r}
mask_n(sum(d$REC_DEATH_DT_COMPOSITE > d$TFL_LAFUDATE, na.rm = TRUE))
```

`add_time_to_event_outcomes()` offers two consistent choices through
`death_window`. The default, `"follow_up"`, counts deaths on or before the
last follow-up date and censors everyone else there. `"ascertainment"`
shares the principle of the SRTR program-specific reports: deaths from any
source count up to an ascertainment date, and everyone else is assumed
alive and censored at that date. In SRTR's words, patients "not reported to
have died in any source are assumed to be alive"
([SRTR Technical Methods](#ref-psr)). Take the date from your SAF release
notes.

It does not reproduce the published patient survival estimates. Those
draw on death sources that `srtr_composite_death()` does not combine, and
report survival at fixed times after transplant; see [SRTR Technical Methods for the
Program-Specific Reports, Section C](https://srtr.hrsa.gov/transplant-professionals/program-specific-report/technical-methods-for-the-program-specific-reports/).

```{r}
out_ascertainment <- sRtr:::add_time_to_event_outcomes(
  tx,
  death_window = "ascertainment",
  ascertainment_date = "YYYY-MM-DD" # from the release notes
)
```

# Graft failure and death on the same day

Graft failure (`TFL_GRAFT_DT`) is often dated on the day of death. The data
dictionary does not say whether that date is filled in with the death date
when a recipient dies with a working graft, or marks a real failure.

SRTR's reports count death as graft failure ("for all organs, deaths are
considered to be graft failures"). They also count retransplant as graft
failure for every organ except heart-lung and lung
([SRTR Technical Methods](#ref-psr);
[Kim and Snyder 2012](#ref-kim2012), slide 27). sRtr dates graft failure
from `TFL_GRAFT_DT` alone, and does not yet use the retransplant date
(`PERS_RETX`). The earlier of `TFL_GRAFT_DT` and death is therefore a
narrower end point than SRTR's graft failure: it misses a retransplant
that came first, or dates it too late. To follow SRTR's definition, take
the earliest of the recorded failure, the retransplant date and death,
inside the observation window. Lung and heart-lung leave out retransplant,
and heart uses only death and retransplant. For heart, SRTR also does not
stop at the last OPTN follow-up date: deaths and retransplants after it
still count, up to the reporting time point
([SRTR Technical Methods](#ref-psr)). Combining events this way is a
modeling choice: a composite end point disregards the possibility that the
exposure affects its parts differently
([Sapir-Pichhadze et al. 2016](#ref-sapir)).

sRtr treats graft failure as death-censored: a failure dated after death
does not count, and a graft without a failure is censored at the earlier of
its last follow-up date and death. By default, a failure on the day of
death counts as death with a working graft (`graft_death_same_day =
"censor"`). That is a package assumption, not an SRTR rule, so run both:

```{r}
as_event <- sRtr:::add_time_to_event_outcomes(tx, graft_death_same_day = "event")
```

# Rejection after the graft has failed

Follow-up forms keep coming after a graft fails: SRTR files forms for the
years after graft failure (`TFL_FOL_CD` codes 801 to 850). A rejection
reported on one of them is about a graft that has already failed, so it is
not an event for a graft-rejection outcome. Neither is a rejection on an
ordinary form dated after the failure.

**The naive approach** takes the first rejection on any form, and censors
rejection-free grafts at last follow-up, past the failure.

**With sRtr**, `add_time_to_event_outcomes()` leaves out the post-failure
forms and ends the rejection window at the graft failure date, by default.
The form filed at failure (code 800) still counts, since it may report the
rejection that caused the failure. Compare with every form counted:

```{r}
keep <- sRtr:::add_time_to_event_outcomes(tx, rejection_after_graft_failure = "keep")
mask_n(sum(keep$FIRST_REJ_DATE_BINARY %in% 1L & !out$FIRST_REJ_DATE_BINARY %in% 1L))
```

# Whose follow-up?

Some outcomes belong to the patient and some to the graft. Malignancy and
death use the patient's last follow-up date; graft failure and rejection
use the graft's. In most files these are the same date. In kidney-pancreas
files (`TX_KP`) each graft has its own last follow-up date
(`TFL_LAFUDATEKI`, `TFL_LAFUDATEPA`), so sRtr gives rejection and graft
failure one set of columns per graft, and uses the later of the two dates
for patient outcomes. A rejection reported on the kidney's form does not
count for the pancreas, and a kidney form saying "no rejection" does not
bound a pancreas rejection.

# Checklist

- Count an event only inside the window the person or graft was followed
  for, and censor everyone else at the end of the same window.
- Use a time-to-event helper that knows the window, or check your dates
  first: `srtr_time_to_event()` trusts what it is given.
- Decide what to do with reports dated on the day of death: keep the
  cohort and follow-up time fixed, reclassify only those events, and run the
  analysis both ways.
- Use one death date consistently, know its source, and look at how far
  apart the sources are.
- Count deaths and censor survivors over the same period: `death_window`.
- Run graft failure both ways for failures on the day of death.
- Stop counting rejection when the graft fails.
- For kidney-pancreas, use each graft's own follow-up.
